summary: This document describes the conventions for using various cryptographic algorithms with the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP), which handles the lifecycle of X.509 certificates. It also updates the algorithm profile in Appendix D.2 of RFC 4210.

eli5.summary: A certificate office needs to know which locks and stamps it may use. This lists the ones to use and how to use them.

subtitle: A current shopping list of cryptographic algorithms for CMP, replacing the aging list in RFC 4210.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) lists mandatory algorithms in Appendix D.2 of RFC 4210, but some of them have weakened over time and should no longer be used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9481 lists current digest, signature, key management, content-encryption and MAC algorithms with their object identifiers and conventions, and gives updated algorithm use profiles.
tldr.outcome: It updates Appendix D.2 of RFC 4210 and gives the Lightweight CMP Profile a list of algorithms it MAY support, so the list can be maintained without rewriting CMP itself.

today: RFC 9481 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It updates RFC 4210, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Algorithm List Needed Updating
sections.content:
Appendix D.2 of RFC 4210 contains a set of algorithms that implementations of the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) are required to support. They were appropriate when CMP was released, but algorithms weaken over time as cryptanalysis improves and computing power grows, so some of them should no longer be used.

RFC 9481 lists current algorithms that can be used with CMP. The stated goal is an easier way to maintain the list of suitable algorithms over time. The document points to ASN.1 values and types from CMP, from CRMF (RFC 4211), from CMP Updates (RFC 9480) and from the Cryptographic Message Syntax. For each algorithm it gives the object identifier (OID), says which protocol fields carry the identifier or the output value, and refers to the RFC that holds the detailed conventions.
sections.eli5: The old list of approved locks was written long ago, and some of those locks are now easy to break. This document is the fresh list.

sections.title: Digests and Signatures
sections.content:
Message digests come in two families. SHA2 gives SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. SHAKE gives SHAKE128 and SHAKE256, which are extendable-output functions. Because the SHA-3 standard prohibits using SHAKE as a general-purpose hash, CMP says the output length MUST be 256 bits for SHAKE128 and 512 bits for SHAKE256.

Signature algorithms protect messages and prove possession of keys. The RFC covers RSA (both RSASSA-PSS and PKCS #1 version 1.5), ECDSA with the NIST-recommended curves, and EdDSA. Each is paired with SHA2 or SHAKE variants, each with its own OID. Ed25519 MUST be used with SHA-512 and Ed448 MUST be used with SHAKE256.

One detail is easy to miss. The hash used to calculate the certHash in certConf messages MUST be SHA512 if the certificate was signed using Ed25519, or SHAKE256 with d=512 if it was signed using Ed448.
sections.eli5: A digest is a short fingerprint of a message. A signature is like signing your name so others know it was really you. This part lists which fingerprint and signing styles are allowed.

sections.title: Key Management and Content Encryption
sections.content:
Sometimes CMP must deliver a private key or other secret. It does this with CMS EnvelopedData, which uses one of three key management techniques: key agreement, key transport, or passwords. RFC 9480 and RFC 4211 promote EnvelopedData by deprecating EncryptedValue.

  • Key agreement: Diffie-Hellman MUST be used only in ephemeral-static variants, and static-static variants SHALL NOT be used. ECDH may use the ephemeral-static variant or 1-Pass ECMQV, again never static-static, and X25519 and X448 are also listed.
  • Key transport: RSA, either PKCS #1 v1.5 or RSAES-OAEP.
  • Key wrap and derivation: AES key wrap protects the content-encryption key, and PBKDF2 derives keys from passwords.

The key wrap and the content-encryption algorithm MUST use the same underlying AES key size, for example AES-128 key wrap with AES-128 content encryption. Content encryption itself uses AES-CBC with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys, and carries things like a signed private key package, a certificate for implicit proof-of-possession, or a revocation passphrase.
sections.eli5: To mail a secret safely you put it in a locked box and then protect the key to that box. This part lists the ways to hand over the box key and which box locks to use.

sections.title: Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
A message authentication code (MAC) protects CMP messages when both sides share a secret instead of using certificates. The RFC lists two password-based options. PasswordBasedMac is the original CMP algorithm. PBMAC1 from PKCS #5 combines a password-based key derivation function such as PBKDF2 with a symmetric MAC.

The underlying symmetric MACs are SHA2-based HMAC, AES-GMAC and SHAKE-based KMAC. AES-GMAC comes with a hard rule: it MUST NOT be used twice with the same parameter set, especially the same nonce, so it MUST NOT be used together with PBKDF2. With PBMAC1 it may only serve as the message authentication scheme, never for the key derivation function.
sections.eli5: A shared secret handshake proves a message came from a friend. This part lists the handshakes that are safe and warns that one of them breaks if you reuse it.

sections.title: Algorithm Use Profiles
sections.content:
The RFC sorts algorithms by bits of security. If an implementation intends to manage certificates for keys of a specific strength, it SHALL implement and use algorithms of at least that strength. If one row does not provide a suitable algorithm, the implementer MUST choose one offering more bits of security. The overall strength is that of the weakest algorithm in the profile.

For the profile in RFC 4210 Appendix D.2, the new table names the algorithms by role. The mandatory choices are RSA (sha256WithRSAEncryption with 2048 bit), PBMAC1, DH, AES-wrap and AES-CBC. It is RECOMMENDED to prefer PBMAC1 over PasswordBasedMac. Deprecated algorithms that SHOULD NOT be used any more include DSA, combinations with MD5 and SHA-1, X9.9, 3-DES, RC5 and CAST-128.

For the Lightweight CMP Profile (RFC 9483) the RFC deliberately does not mandate a set, because the right set depends on the operations implemented and the certificates involved. It gives a table of examples for each role instead.
sections.eli5: Your chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so you should pick locks that are all about equally strong. The mandatory list says which ones every office must have.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The algorithms to be supported heavily depend on the certificates and PKI management operations in the target environment. The algorithm with the lowest security strength and the entropy of any shared secret define the security of the overall solution.

When using MAC-based protection, PBMAC1 is preferable to PasswordBasedMac. PBMAC1 is a well-known, scrutinized algorithm, while PasswordBasedMac is essentially PBKDF1 with an HMAC step at the end. PBKDF1 is not recommended for new applications and is no longer approved by most standards bodies, which makes certification difficult for implementers.

Older CMP implementations that follow Appendix D.2 may exist, for example with 3-DES mandatory for PROT_SYM_ALG while AES is now mandatory. Weakened algorithms should be disabled, and critical systems that cannot be updated at once should adopt a plan to migrate as soon as possible. The RFC also notes that AES-GMAC must not be the pseudorandom function in PBKDF2.
sections.eli5: If one lock in a row of locks is weak, a burglar picks that one. So retire the old weak locks, and plan a swap soon if you cannot do it today.
